In summary, our research is concerned with
the use of epicardial ablation to create transmural lesions in patients with AF who have failed prior attempts at endocardial isolation.
the use of epicardial catheter ablation to complete electrical isolation of the posterior LA wall.
the development of an innovative approach to the treatment of AF, the “Box” lesion set, and the use of epicardial ablation as an adjunctive therapy to complete a posterior box lesion.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the epicardial ablation approach is a viable option to achieve complete posterior box lesions and electrical isolation of the PVs.
the posterior box lesion set can be achieved by epicardial catheter ablation in patients with persistent AF.

the use of epicardial ablation is not required to create a posterior box lesion, but it is a safe, feasible, and effective option in cases wherein endocardial ablation is unable to achieve the desired lesion set.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the combined endo‐and epicardial approach can be used to achieve electrical isolation of the PVs and posterior LA wall.

the combined epicardial and endocardial approach to create an electrical box lesion set can be effective for the treatment of persistent AF, and should be considered for those patients who have failed prior ablation attempts.
the combined endocardial–epicardial approach is an important adjunct to the endocardial approach in the creation of the “box” lesion.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the use of an epicardial approach to complete a box lesion set is feasible, and can be used in select patients who have persistent or long‐standing persistent AF, or who have had prior ablation procedures.
the epicardial approach can be an effective and safe adjunct to create an electric isolation of the PVs in cases wherein endocardial isolation alone is insufficient.
in patients with a large posterior LA, a combined epicardial and endocardial ablation strategy can be a safe and effective means to create a posterior box lesion set.
